reference: Abara, N., Hollis, T. (2019). Ownership and exit in municipal volunteer programs. Journal of Civic Administration. doi:10.5555/jca.2019.0142
sentence: In a panel of 48 city programs, 31% of first-year volunteers left before completing six months of service [@abara2019, p. 7].
source_text:
Ownership and exit in municipal volunteer programs
Nkem Abara and Teresa Hollis (SYNTHETIC)

[p. 5]
We followed every volunteer who joined one of the programs in our panel during a single recruitment year and recorded the date of their last logged shift.

[p. 7]
Across the 48 programs in our panel, 31% of first-year volunteers exited before completing six months of service. Exit was concentrated in the first eight weeks.

reference: Castellanos, R., Ibe, K. (2017). Fit and retention in local volunteering. Voluntary Sector Studies. doi:10.5555/vss.2017.0021
sentence: Castellanos and Ibe describe retention as a matter of fit between the volunteer's goals and the tasks offered [@castellanos2017].

reference: Moreno, L. (2018). Matching volunteers to roles. Civic Press. doi:10.5555/cp.2018.0011
sentence: Moreno calls this the "role-match problem" and argues that it is invisible in sign-up data [@moreno2018, p. 33].
source_text:
Matching Volunteers to Roles
Lucia Moreno (SYNTHETIC)

[p. 33]
I call this the role-match problem: the tasks a program needs done and the tasks volunteers came to do drift apart. Because sign-up forms record availability rather than purpose, the role-match problem is invisible in sign-up data.

reference: de Vries, M. (2021). Scheduling flexibility and volunteer hours. Nonprofit Management Review. doi:10.5555/nmr.2021.0120
sentence: Flexible scheduling was associated with more hours per volunteer but not with longer tenure [@devries2021].
source_text:
Scheduling flexibility and volunteer hours
Maarten de Vries (SYNTHETIC)

[p. 14]
Volunteers offered flexible schedules contributed more hours per month, but their tenure did not differ from that of volunteers on fixed schedules.

reference: Whitlock, G. (2020). Named contacts and volunteer tenure in three cities. Urban Affairs Notes. doi:10.5555/uan.2020.0230
sentence: Whitlock found that assigning a named staff contact kept volunteers longer in two of the three cities studied [@whitlock2020, p. 112].
source_text:
Named contacts and volunteer tenure in three cities
Grace Whitlock (SYNTHETIC)

[p. 112]
In two of the three cities, volunteers assigned a named staff contact stayed longer than those without one. In the third city the difference was small and not statistically significant.
